Thereafter, the said Hereinafter referred to as the 'suit property' Pakkirappa filed EP No.52/63 to execute the decree passed in the said suit.
During the pendency of the execution proceedings, M.Pakkirappa died and his children came on record as his legal representatives and prosecuted the said proceedings.

The defendants admit the family partition in the year 1961.

However, it is their specific contention that though there was a partition in the family in the year 1961, the plaintiff and defendants along with their mother Laxmamma continued to live jointly up to 1967-68 and that after attaining majority, the defendants started livingly separately and while separating from the family there was an oral division of the properties which were purchased under the execution proceedings and the suit property measuring an extent of 4.61 acres and the house situated in it fell to the share of defendant Nos.1 and 2.
That on the basis of the oral partition/division effected in the family in the year 1967-68, the defendants continued to cultivate the said land as owners from the date of partition i.e., 1967-68.
That the respective properties purchased under the execution case fell to the share of the plaintiff.
That the portion acquired by the Railway Department fell to the share of the plaintiff and he received the entire compensation for the same.
That a portion of the property that fell to the share of the plaintiff was sold by making plots.

Hence, it is contended that the plaintiff has no right or title over the suit property after the division in the year 1967-68 and in fact, it is the defendant Nos.1 and 2 who are the absolute owners of the suit property and in lawful possession of the same.
It is further contended that the record of rights of the said property stands in the name of defendant Nos.1 and 2 since 1967-68 till date.
Defendant No.1 denied the assertion of the plaintiff that defendant Nos.1 and 2 attempted to disturb the possession and enjoyment of the plaintiff in the suit property.

sentences.text: The submissions of both the learned counsel have been considered and the material available on record has been perused including the records of the Trial Court and the first appellate Court.
21. Before noticing the contentions put forth by both the parties, it is relevant to notice the findings recorded by both the Courts.

22. The Trial Court, while considering additional issue Nos.1 and 2 has recorded the following findings:
i.

It is an admitted fact that Ex.P4 - the Sale Certificate is issued by the Court in favour of the plaintiff;
ii.
It is admitted by both the parties that the partition took place pertaining to the other properties between them through registered Partition Deed (Ex.P3) during the lifetime of Pakkirappa;

iii. Though in Ex.P4 it has not specifically mentioned that the plaintiff purchased the suit property on behalf of the other decree holders, when the legal representatives of Pakkirappa were on record, it can be presumed that the properties which were purchased in the public auction as per Ex.P4 are the joint family properties;
iv. Except the Sale Certificate (Ex.P4), no iota of document is produced by the plaintiff to show that he is in actual possession and enjoyment of the suit property.
v. The only document relied on by the plaintiff is Ex.P20 -Record of rights pertaining to the suit property which is standing in his name on the basis of ME No.27/2000.

The mutation entry has been challenged by the defendants before the Assistant Commissioner, wherein the said order passed by the Tahsildar has been set aside;
vi.

On perusal of Ex.P27 which is a proceeding of the Tahsildar, Hospet dated 28.2.2001, the Tahsildar on the basis of the application of the plaintiff has mutated the immovable property in the name of the plaintiff on the basis of the Sale Certificate (Ex.P4).

The order of the Tahsildar (Ex.P27) has been set aside by the order of the Assistant Commissioner (Ex.D1) and the Assistant Commissioner has directed both the parties to approach the Civil Court and adjudicate their rights;
vii.
It is admitted fact that OS No.7/1962 was filed by the father of the plaintiff.
It is also admitted fact that by order dated 22.11.1962 passed on an IA, the plaintiff and defendant Nos.1 and 2 who were the legal heirs of Pakkirappa have been brought on record.

If they were not living together after 1961 as alleged by the plaintiff, there is no explanation as to how the plaintiff and defendants came on record in EP No.52/63 as legal heirs of deceased Pakkirappa;
viii.

sentences.text: The defendants have established the contention about the existence of undivided Hindu joint family till 1967- 68; x.

On perusal of record of rights which are marked as Exs.D15 to D17 pertaining to the suit property from 1967-68 to 2000-01, the same clearly goes to show that the name of the defendants has appeared in column Nos. 9 and 12 and nowhere in the said document the name of the plaintiff is entered that he is also the owner of the suit properties along with the defendants;
xi.

On perusal of the evidence of the defendants, they have established that there was an undivided Hindu joint family and the suit property has been allotted to the share of defendants and therefore,
their names are found in column Nos.9 and 12 in Exs.D15 to D20.
It further goes to show that the plaintiff has kept quite since 1964 to 1999.
That and in the year 1999, the plaintiff abruptly approached the Tahsildar and filed an application for effecting change of katha pertaining to the suit property on the basis of the Sale Certificate.
xii. PW.1 in his cross- examination admitted that the father of the defendants died even prior to the death of his father and his father died in the year 1963.
He further admitted the partition in the year 1961 during the lifetime of his father and at that time, all the children of his father had acquired share in the properties.
He also admitted that as the father of the defendants was not alive at the time of partition and his share was apportioned amongst the defendants and the guardian of their mother Laxmavva.

He admitted that after the decree passed in OS No.71/1962 his father died and himself and other children of his father including the defendants jointly filed EP No.52/63;
xiii.
The defendants have established that they lived jointly with the plaintiff from 1967-68 though partition took place pertaining to the suit property in the year 1961.

The defendants have established that the suit properties have been purchased on behalf of the joint family and it is not the self acquired property of the plaintiff;
xiv.

In support of their contention regarding the oral partition in the year 1967-68, defendant No.1 examined himself as DW.1, the mother of the plaintiff has been examined as DW.2 and son of the brother of the plaintiff has been examined as DW.3;
xv. The son of the plaintiff though examined as PW.2 he has not supported the version of the plaintiff.

DWs.2 and 3 have deposed that at the time of division of the properties in the year 1961 father of defendant Nos.1 and 2 was not alive together were allotted share by making their mother as natural guardian.

Further, they deposed that after the partition in the year 1961, they started living separately and since defendant No.1 had just attained majority and defendant No.2 was minor, the plaintiff and defendants continued to live jointly up to 1967-68.

That during the time of joint family, the suit property and other properties were in joint cultivation of the plaintiff and defendants and in the year 1967-68, defendant Nos.1 and 2 and plaintiff have divided.
In the said oral partition the properties which have been purchased in the Court auction had been included in the oral partition.

Mabavva out of RS No.63A of P.K.Halli through registered Sale Deed Ex.D21/P9 and the plaintiff has subscribed his signature as an attesting witness admitting the ownership of the defendant in RS No.63 P.K.Halli;

Even otherwise, he had no explanation why the names of defendant Nos.1 and 2 have appeared in RTC since 1967-68 till 1999;

The additional issue regarding the suit being barred by limitation, is answered in the affirmative since in the year 1972 itself, the defendant has executed the Sale Deed in respect of a portion of the suit property in favour of Mabavva under a registered Deed.

Therefore, the plaintiff ought to have filed a suit for declaration within three years from the date of execution of the Sale Deed by defendants in favour of Mabavva;
xxii.
The plaintiff has produced Tax paid receipts (Ex.P1) pertaining to the year 2004.

He has not at all produced any document to show that he is paying taxes to the suit property since 1963;

The plaintiff has not produced any document to show that he is in possession of the suit property since 1963;

However, this document has been issued on the basis of the order passed by the Tahsildar (Ex.P27);
23.
While considering issue Nos.1 and 2, the Trial Court has answered the same in the negative that the plaintiff has failed to prove lawful possession to the suit property.
24. The first appellate Court upon a re-appreciation of the oral and documentary evidence on record, has affirmed the findings of the Trial Court.

Further, the first appellate Court has noticed that if at all the plaintiff alone purchased the property in the Court auction, there was no necessity for the plaintiff to permit the defendants to cultivate the land and there is no explanation as to how the names of the defendants have been entered in the revenue records and that the same clearly shows that the property has fallen to the share of the defendants and they are cultivating separately.

25. Having regard to the findings recorded by both the Courts and noticing the contentions put forth by both the Counsels, it is relevant to note that there is no dispute about the fact that by a registered Partition Deed dated 25.10.1961 which was entered into during the lifetime of the father of the plaintiff namely, Pakkirappa, his properties were divided amongst his children.
It is further not in dispute that said Pakkirappa filed OS No.7/62, which was decreed and thereafter, EP No.52/63 was filed to execute the said decree.
That upon the death of Pakkirappa his legal heirs have come on record in the said execution proceedings.

It is also not in dispute that the Sale Certificate (Ex.P4)
issued in respect of the property sold in the public auction is standing solely in the name of the plaintiff.

26. It is relevant to note that under Ex.P4 three items of properties have been purchased i.e., an extent of 0.34 acres in Sy.No.59/A, an extent of 1.94 acres in Sy.No.63/A and an extent of 5.78 acres and one building situated in Papinayakanahalli in Sy.No.63.
The total extent of property purchased was 8.06 acres.

The suit property is an extent of 4.61 acres in Sy.No.63A/1.
27.
It is the case of the plaintiff that the property purchased vide Ex.P4 is his absolute property.
However, the defendants have specifically pleaded that there was a family partition in the year 1961.

That the plaintiff and defendants along with their mother Lakshmamma were continued to live together upto the year 1967-68 and after the defendants attained the age of majority they started living separately from the plaintiff and while separating, there was an oral division of the properties which were purchased in the execution proceedings.
That the suit property measuring an extent of 4.61 acres and the house situated in it fell to the share of the defendants.
That on the basis of the oral partition effected in the year 1967-68, the defendants continued to cultivate the suit property as its owners from the said date till date.

He is also been cross examined.
The plaintiff examined his son from his first wife as PW.2.

However,
PW.2 has not supported the case of the plaintiff.
The defendant No.1 examined himself as DW.1.
The brother of the plaintiff has been examined as DW.2 and the son of the elder brother of the plaintiff has been examined as DW.3.

The Trial Court has recorded a finding that having regard to the testimony of DWs.2 and 3 as well as the other material on record, the defendants have established that there was an oral partition in the year 1967-68 pertaining to the property purchased in the Court auction though registered partition took place in the year 1961.
29. Learned counsel for the appellant vehemently contends that oral partition is required to be strictly proved.

In support of his contention, he relies on the following judgments:
29.1.

The Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of Bhagavati Prasad Shah5 held as follows:
"10.

Before we discuss the evidence on the record, we desire to point out that on the admitted facts of this case neither party has any presumption on his side either as regards the jointness or separation of the family.

The general principle undoubtedly is that a Hindu family is presumed to be joint unless the contrary is proved, but where it is admitted that one of the coparceners did separate himself from the other members of the joint family and had his share in the joint property partitioned off for him, there is no presumption that the rest of the coparceners continued to be joint.
There is no presumption on the other side too that because one member of the family separated himself, there has been separation with regard to all.

It would be a question of fact to be determined in each case upon the evidence relating to the intention of the parties whether there was a separation amongst the other coparceners or that they remained united.
The burden would undoubtedly lie on the party who asserts the existence of a particular state of things on the basis of which he claims relief.

These principles which have been laid down in several pronouncements of the Judicial Committee seem to us to be perfectly sound (vide Bal Krishna v. Ram Krishna [Bal Krishna v. Ram Krishna, (1930-31) 58 IA 220 : 1931 SCC OnLine PC 31]
and Palani Ammal v. Muthuvenkatachala Moniagar [Palani Ammal v.
Muthuvenkatachala Moniagar, (1924-25) 52 IA 83 : 1924 SCC OnLine PC 61] and Balabux Ladhuram v. Rukhmabai [Balabux Ladhuram v. Rukhmabai, (1902-03) 30 IA 130 : 1903 SCC OnLine PC 10] ).

sentences.text: Another thing to be noted in this connection is that it is not the case of the defendants made either in the pleadings or in the evidence that even if there was a separation between Ram Narain and Ram Saran at any anterior time they subsequently reunited.
The controversy, therefore, narrows down to the short point as to whether at any time before the death of Ram Narain there was a separation between him and Ram Saran.

If, as the plaintiff avers, there was a disruption of the joint status in regard to all the three brothers, it would really be immaterial if, subsequent to separation, Ram Narain and Ram Saran lived together in commensality or dealt with their properties in such manner as is ordinarily done by members of a joint Hindu family which is not set up in the present Sri M Pampapathy @ Pampanna vs Sri M Sanna Pampapathy on 13 September, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/56996482/
13 case.

entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Except in the case of reunion, the mere fact that separated coparceners chose to live together or act jointly for purposes of business or trade or in their dealings with properties, would not give them the status of coparceners under the Mitakshara law.

It is in the light of these principles that we propose to examine the evidence before us."
(emphasis supplied) 29.2.

The Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of Bhagavan Dayal6 has held as follows:
"21.
The next question is whether there was a reunion between Kashi Ram, Raghubar Dayal and Bhagwan Dayal.

The learned Attorney-General contends that on the assumption that there was a partition of the family, the consistent conduct of the parties for a period of 50 years unambiguously establishes that there was a reunion between Kashi Ram, Raghubar Dayal and Bhagwan Dayal during the lifetime of Kashi Ram, or at any rate there was a reunion after the death of Kashi Ram between Raghubar Dayal and Bhagwan Dayal.

Mr Viswanatha Sastri, on the other hand,
argues that when there was a partition in the family, the members of the family who allege a reunion must strictly prove the same, and that the documentary evidence filed in this case spread over a long period of time is destructive of any such claim.

22. For the correct approach to this question, it would be convenient to quote at the outset the observations of the Judicial Committee in Palani Ammal v.
Muthuvenkatacharla Moniagar [(1924) LR 52 IA 83, 86] :
"It is also quite clear that if a joint Hindu family separates, the family or any members of it may agree to reunite as a joint Hindu family, but such a reuniting is for obvious reasons, which would apply in many cases under the law of the Mitakshara,
of very rare occurrence, and when it happens it must be strictly proved as any other disputed fact is proved.

Muthuvenkatacharla Moniagar [(1924) LR 52 IA 83, 86]

sentences.text: It is also well settled that to constitute a reunion there must be an intention of the parties to reunite in estate and interest.

It is implicit in the concept of a reunion that there shall be an agreement between the parties to reunite in estate with an intention to revert to their former status of members of a joint Hindu family.
Such an agreement need not be express, but may be implied from the conduct of the parties alleged to have reunited.
But the conduct must be of such an incontrovertible character that an agreement of reunion must be necessarily implied therefrom.
As the burden is heavy on a party asserting reunion, ambiguous pieces of conduct equally consistent with a reunion or ordinary joint enjoyment cannot sustain a plea of reunion.

The legal position has been neatly summarized in Mayne's Hindu law, 11th Edn., thus at p. 569:
Sri M Pampapathy @ Pampanna vs Sri M Sanna Pampapathy on 13 September, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/56996482/
14

entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: "As the presumption is in favour of union until a partition is made out, so after a partition the presumption would be against a reunion.

To establish it, it is necessary to show, not only that the parties already divided, lived or traded together, but that they did so with the intention of thereby altering their status and of forming a joint estate with all its usual incidents.

It requires very cogent evidence to satisfy the burden of establishing that by agreement between them, the divided members of a joint Hindu family have succeeded in so altering their status as to bring themselves within all the rights and obligations that follow from the fresh formation of a joint undivided Hindu family."
As we give our full assent to these observations, we need not pursue the matter with further citations except to consider two decisions strongly relied upon by the learned Attorney-General.
Venkataramayya v. Tatayya [AIR 1943 Mad 538] is a decision of a Division Bench of the Madras High Court.

It was pointed out there that "mere jointness in residence, food or worship or a mere trading together cannot bring about the conversion of the divided status into a joint one with all the usual incidents of jointness in estate and interest unless an intention to become reunited in the sense of the Hindu law is clearly established".
The said proposition is unexceptionable, and indeed that is the well settled law.
But on the facts of that case, the learned Judges came to the conclusion that there was a reunion.
The partition there was effected between a father and his sons by the first wife.
One of the sons was a minor.
The question was whether there was a reunion between the brothers soon after the alleged partition.

The learned Judges held that as between the sons there was never any reason for separation inter se, and that the evidence disclosed that on their conduct no explanation other than reunion was possible.
They also pointed out that though at the time of partition one of the brothers was a minor, after he attained majority, he accepted the position of reunion.

The observations relied upon by the learned Attorney- General read thus:
"In our view, it is not necessary that there should be a formal and express agreement to reunite.
Such an agreement can be established by clear evidence of conduct incapable of explanation on any other footing."
This principle also is unexceptionable.
But the facts of that case are entirely different from those in the present case, and the conclusion arrived at by the learned Judges cannot help us in arriving at a finding in the instant case."
(emphasis supplied)

30. The defendants in the present case have specifically pleaded reunion inasmuch as, they have specifically pleaded that despite the registered partition dated 25.10.1961, since the father of the defendants had died and since defendant No.1 had just attained majority and defendant No.2 was still a minor, they along with their mother continued to live along with the plaintiff.
That after the defendants attained majority in the year 1967-68, they started residing separately and at that time there was an oral partition of the property purchased under Ex.P4.

Consistent with the case putforth by the defendants, it is forthcoming from the material on record that from the property purchased under Ex.P4, an extent of 1.90 cents of land acquired by Railways, which compensation has been Sri M Pampapathy @ Pampanna vs Sri M Sanna Pampapathy on 13 September, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/56996482/
15 paid to the plaintiff and that in a certain portion of the properties acquired under Ex.P4, the plaintiff has formed sites and sold the same.

entities.text: Sri M Pampapathy @ Pampanna vs Sri M Sanna Pampapathy
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Hence, it is the case of the defendants that the suit property is the remaining property from the property purchased under Ex.P4 was allotted to the share of the defendants.
It is the further case of the defendants that they have been cultivating the suit property from the year 1967-68.
The revenue entries i.e., Exs.D15 to D20 - RORs pertaining to the suit property are also standing in the name of the defendants.
Both the courts have recorded concurrent findings holding that the defendants have proved their case.

31. Although, it is the vehement contention of the learned counsel for the appellant-plaintiff that mere entries in the revenue entries do not demonstrate the ownership and that the partition alleged on behalf of the defendants is not registered, it is relevant to note that the defendants have specifically pleaded reunion with the plaintiff after the registered partition dated 25.10.1961 and have also specifically pleaded the subsequent oral partition in the year 1967-68 as well as the circumstances surrounding such an occurrence.
The oral and documentary evidence has also been adduced in support of the same as noticed above.
Further, both the Courts have recorded concurrent findings of fact that the suit property has been allotted to the share of the defendants.

It is relevant to note that having regard to the position of law as held in the cases of Bhagavati Prasad Shah and others5 and Bhagavan Dayal6, the defendants have specifically pleaded re- union and they have also adduced sufficient evidence to prove the same.
32.

Although it is the vehement contention of the learned counsel for the appellant/plaintiff that the suit property is the absolute property of the plaintiff having regard to the specific plea of the defendants as noticed above as also in view of the oral and documentary evidence on record as well as the concurrent findings recorded by both the Courts, the plaintiff has failed to demonstrate that the said concurrent findings are in any manner erroneous and liable to be interfered with.

33. With regard to the substantial question of law framed vide order dated 02.09.2009, it is relevant to note that the Trial Court has recorded a finding that the suit is barred by limitation merely on the basis that the plaintiff has signed as a witness to the Sale Deed in the year 1972.
It is forthcoming that the Sale Deed dated 28.03.1972 (Ex.P9) has merely been referred to in the examination-in-chief of PW.1 that he is not bound by the said document.
There is no pleading of either of the parties with regard to the said Sale Deed (Ex.P9).
The first appellate Court has also not considered the aspect regarding the finding of the trial Court that the suit is barred by limitation.
In view of the same, the finding of the Trial Court on limitation is erroneous and liable to be set aside.
34. In view of the discussion made above, the substantial questions of law framed on 02.09.2009 and on 18.7.2024 are answered in the negative.

Accordingly, the following:
ORDER i) The above appeal is dismissed.
